newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean opposition slams president's apology.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean opposition slams president's apology.

text.p: South Korea's main opposition leader Kim Dae-jung on Friday blasted President Kim Young-sam's apology over financial abuses as "pompous and confrontational" and said he had evidence of wrongdoing.
He vowed a head-on fight with the president to uncover the truth behind his spending on the 1992 presidential election.

Kim Dae-jung, who heads the National Congress for New Politics, alleged President Kim received 300 billion won ($336 million) from his predecessor Roh Tae-woo and 60 billion won from the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group.
The spending limit for candidates in the 1992 elections, in which Kim Dae-jung was defeated, was 36.7 billion won.
"I have evidence and witnesses, but they cannot come forward yet," the opposition firebrand told a news conference.
Roh is serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and other crimes while in office. Hanbo is at the centre of a bribery scandal engulfing Kim Young-sam's own presidency.

"His gesture, tone of voice, and the content of his speech were pompous and confrontational," said Kim Dae-jung, elected by his party last week to be its standard-bearer in presidential elections in December.

President Kim apologised in a live national television broadcast for "past wrongdoings" by himself and others. But he refused to give any specifics and suggested his opponents were just as guilty. He also promised reform of election spending legislation.

"I know the president is smart. Why would he not remember receiving money from Roh Tae-woo and Hanbo?" asked Kim Dae-jung, whose rivalry with the president has overshadowed South Korean politics for several decades.
"We cannot tolerate this any more. We have decided to fight the president directly," he said, adding his party would demand an independent probe by the National Assembly.
However, Kim Dae-jung said there were no immediate plans to call on the president to step down before his single term expires in February next year.

Asked about his own election funding, Kim Dae-jung said: "Kim Young-sam used so much he doesn't know how much he used. But we are are poor and we know exactly how much we spent." He put his own spending at 20.7 billion won.
Civic groups also lashed out at the president's apology.

The Citizens' Coalition for Economic Justice said in a statement: "The people yearned for political reform based on a truthful speech, but the president has completely ignored that and has disappointed the people and failed to persuade them."
The militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, South Korea's second largest umbrella organisation, demanded a full apology and an account of the president's 1992 spending.
"He must reveal in detail the content and size of his election funds and bow his head and apologise to the people," it said in a statement.
The Federation of Korean Industries, which represents big business groups, gave a guarded welcome to the speech.
"It is positive that the president acknowledged the mistake and tried to gain the understanding of the people and put an end to the issue," it said in a statement. ($1=892 won)
